# Architecture rules

Reviews module boundaries, dependency direction and coupling across the codebase, starting from the import graph.

- Agent id: `architecture`
- Rules: 14 (source: [`architecture.yaml`](https://github.com/adryserage/aetheris/blob/main/aetheris/rules/architecture.yaml))
- Deterministic checks: `circular_imports`

## ARC-001: Circular dependency between modules

- Severity: medium
- Languages: all
- References: CWE-1047

Look for import cycles between modules or packages, starting with the cycles the import graph check reports, and name the import that should be removed or inverted to break each one. Raise it to high when the cycle causes an import-time error or partial initialization. Imports done only for type checking (`if TYPE_CHECKING:`, `import type`) and a lazy import inside a function used to break a known cycle are not cycles at runtime; report those as low only when the cycle shows a misplaced type.

## ARC-002: Dependency points the wrong way

- Severity: medium
- Languages: all

Look for low-level or core modules (domain models, utilities, data access) importing from higher layers (HTTP handlers, CLI commands, UI components), and for a domain module importing a web framework or database driver directly. Infer the layers from the folder layout and the project's own docs; do not report a direction the project clearly chose on purpose, such as an adapter package that imports the framework.

## ARC-003: Business logic inside transport or UI code

- Severity: medium
- Languages: all

Look for route handlers, controllers, CLI commands or UI components that hold pricing, validation, state transitions or data rules longer than a few lines instead of calling a function that can be tested without the framework. Handlers that only parse input, call one service function and format the response are the expected shape.

## ARC-004: Data access outside the data layer

- Severity: medium
- Languages: all
- References: CWE-1057

Look for raw SQL, ORM sessions or HTTP clients to the project's own storage used directly from views, templates or UI components when the codebase has a repository or service layer for that data. Small scripts and migrations that query the database directly are not violations.

## ARC-005: God module

- Severity: medium
- Languages: all

Look for a single file or class that many unrelated modules import and that mixes several responsibilities, such as configuration, I/O, formatting and business rules, in one place (often named `utils`, `helpers`, `common`, `manager`). A cohesive module that is large because its one domain is large is not a violation; report what each separate responsibility should become.

## ARC-006: Duplicated logic across modules

- Severity: medium
- Languages: all
- References: CWE-1041

Look for the same algorithm, validation, mapping or constant table implemented in two or more modules so that a change to one copy can silently diverge from the other. Small idiomatic snippets (a three-line guard, standard boilerplate) and generated code are not violations.

## ARC-007: Global mutable state shared across modules

- Severity: high
- Languages: all

Look for module-level mutable objects (dicts, lists, singletons, class attributes) written from several modules or from concurrent requests, threads or tasks without a lock or clear owner. Constants, caches with a single owner and thread-safe primitives, and configuration loaded once at startup and then read only, are not violations.

## ARC-008: Concrete dependency hardwired where tests need a seam

- Severity: low
- Languages: all

Look for functions that construct their own database clients, HTTP clients, clocks or file system access deep inside business logic, so the logic cannot be tested without the real service. Constructing a dependency once at the application entry point and passing it in is the expected pattern; do not ask for an interface when there is only one implementation and the code is already testable.

## ARC-009: Inconsistent interface between modules

- Severity: high
- Languages: all

Look for a caller and a callee in different modules that disagree on a contract, such as argument order or names, the type or shape of a returned object, units, nullability, or the exceptions raised, including imports of names the target module no longer exports. Report both locations.

## ARC-010: Missing or unresolved internal import

- Severity: high
- Languages: all

Look for imports of project modules or files that do not exist at the resolved path, including stale relative imports after a move. Imports of third-party packages that are declared in the manifest, and optional imports guarded by `try/except ImportError`, are not violations.

## ARC-011: Deep inheritance hierarchy

- Severity: low
- Languages: all
- References: CWE-1074

Look for class hierarchies more than three levels deep in project code, or base classes whose subclasses override most methods, where composition would make behavior easier to follow. Hierarchies required by a framework (Django models, exception classes) are not violations.

## ARC-012: Configuration scattered through code

- Severity: medium
- Languages: all

Look for environment variables, URLs, feature flags or limits read in many modules with their own defaults instead of being parsed once into a configuration object at startup. A single settings module that every other module imports is the expected pattern.

## ARC-013: Speculative abstraction

- Severity: low
- Languages: all

Look for interfaces, factories, plugin registries or base classes with exactly one implementation and no stated plan for a second, and for wrapper functions with one caller that only forward their arguments. Abstractions required by a framework, or used to substitute a test double that tests really use, are not violations.

## ARC-014: Error handling strategy differs between layers

- Severity: medium
- Languages: all

Look for layers that mix error styles for the same kind of failure, such as one module returning `None` or error codes while its neighbors raise exceptions, or exceptions from a library leaking through several layers to the user. Converting library errors into the project's own error type at the boundary is the expected pattern.
